I wrote about this in AINews last night but basically https://t.co/bx6aYCqlW8 is gathering the top 1000 AI Engineers to 1) accurately represent the 2026 SOTA in AI x Code, 2) preview 2027.

So proud to have gathered the best collection of invited attendees, speakers and sponsors to reflect the three themes that have defined this year:
Fascinating case study of the sharpest edge of what you can do with agentic engineering in the Fable era - my eyebrows raised at least a dozen times while reading this

It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

Mistral Large 4 OSS debuts at #5 among open-weight models on the Vals Index and #17 overall. 🐈

Its accuracy is comparable to Large 4, but it completes tasks with far fewer tokens and steps. https://t.co/3EBTT7cUcx

Real-world results are in: GPT-6.1 Terra (Max) by @OpenAI ranks #8 in Agent Arena across nearly 9K agentic sessions from our global community of users.

With +10.6% net improvement and a median cost per task of $0.62, it has reshaped the Pareto frontier! See its placement in the thread. Its median cost per task is:

- 43% lower than Gemini 4 Argon (High) at #7 ($1.09)
- 30% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol (Max) at #6 ($0.89)
- 88% lower than GPT-6 Astra (Max) at #5 ($5.16)

By signal, its strengths include:

- #7 in Steerability (+13.3%): whether the model can course-correct when you push back
- #3 in Bash Reliability (+13.2%): whether its commands succeed, excluding errors outside its control
- #9 in Praise vs Complaint (+16.8%): implicit sentiment in users’ reactions

Congrats again to the @OpenAI team on this release!

Lower cost per task doesn’t always come from lower token prices.

On Agent Arena, GPT-6.1 Sol (Max) by @OpenAI costs $1.91 per task:
- 85% less than #1 Claude Opus 5.5 (Max) by @AnthropicAI at $12.51
- 87% less than #3 GPT-6 Astra (Max) by @OpenAI, at $14.93

But these savings come from different places.

Against Astra, Sol’s cost advantage comes primarily from lower token prices. Against Opus, it comes primarily from using fewer tokens per task.

How do we derive this?

Agent Arena tracks real costs of users’ tasks. Cost per task is the tokens a model uses times the price of each token, across input, output and cache-read tokens. By comparing pricing and token counts, we can identify what drives the cost reductions.

Your agent would cost 260% more without the cache.

We analyzed +26K Agent Arena sessions from September 12 to October 23, 2026, spanning 30 agents and 13 labs.

Caching dramatically changes the economics of a typical task. If every cached token were instead billed at the model's full input price, a task sent to one of Agent Arena's top-10 agents would cost 3.6x as much (260% more).

The savings become especially tangible for leading models. A typical Claude Fable 5.1 task costs $7.44 today; without caching, it would cost $27.

Even a coffee break can carry a hidden price: if your cache expires while you’re away, the agent may have to resend the entire conversation at full input price. In our Agent Arena sample, a single cache invalidation translated to a 5% higher bill for a typical task.

Read more findings from our analysis of the hidden AI price war in the article below.

What if AI agents could safely improve their own harness at runtime? UC Berkeley PhD candidate and senior researcher @AlexKrentsel from @GoogleResearch recently presented his work on self-improving AI agents at Arena HQ.

This architecture, Exo, borrows the exokernel idea from operating systems, separating an agent into a protected mechanism layer (state, history, secrets, and a "guardian") and a fully evolvable policy layer.

Alex walks through the design, results on benchmarks and open-world RuneScape tasks, where Exo was 31-62% cheaper than Codex and Pi, and more. 

Big thanks to @AlexKrentsel for joining us to present his work with @istoica05, @martin_casado, @ankrgyl, Sylvia Ratnasamy, @BerkeleySky, and @netsyslab. 

https://t.co/LRNbInTzSn

This Week in the Arena: Gemini is back, and Terra got even more efficient.

- Gemini 4 Carbon (High) by @GoogleDeepmind landed #1 in Text Arena, #2 in Agent Arena, and #4 in Code Arena: WebDev. It reshaped the Pareto frontier across all three arenas. See first impressions from @petergostev in thread below.

- GPT-6.1 Terra (Max) by @OpenAI entered Agent Arena at #8 with +10.6% net improvement at $0.62 median cost per task, reshaping the Pareto frontier and offering price efficiency.

- We introduced Connectors to Agent Mode. Our global community of users can combine tools like Vercel, Linear, GitHub, and more in a single task to complete more complex workflows from start to finish. Details in the thread.
https://t.co/obaBwSIpEC

We've launched our HLE-Diamond leaderboard, our independent evaluation of the refined 1,000-question version of Humanity's Last Exam, as part of v5 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index

HLE-Diamond was released by @CAIS and @scale_AI after a year of cleaning and refining the original Humanity's Last Exam dataset with input from the research community. It has 1,000 closed-ended questions, split evenly between reasoning and knowledge, and 272 of them include an image.

We run every question once without tools, using the official HLE system prompt. GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) grades each answer against the reference answer with the official HLE judge prompt, and we report the share of questions judged correct (pass@1).

Key takeaways:

➤ Only 17 model variants (~13%) score above 50% today: Gemini 4 Carbon (high) leads at 69%, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 68%

➤ Models score higher on reasoning than on knowledge: Over 90% of the models we measured do better on the reasoning portion of the benchmark. Gemini 4 Carbon (high) leads both, at 80% on reasoning and 59% on knowledge. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max) both score 78% on reasoning, and Opus 5.5 is ahead on knowledge, 58% vs 50%

➤ Open weights models trail by more than 30 points: Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released) is the top open weights model at 37%, followed by MiniMax-M3.1-Flash at 28% and Kimi K3 (max) at 27%

In AA-PersonalityBench, each recent Grok release from has become less sycophantic, more sincere, and produces less slop

The Slop trait assesses how much generic filler or AI-flavored padding models use; Sycophantic measures whether models excessively flatter or agree with the user rather than responding honestly; Sincere measures a model’s tonal authenticity, as opposed to forced enthusiasm or templated responses.

Across the last three Grok releases from @elonmusk’s @SpaceXSI, Slop fell 62 percentile points, Sycophantic fell 17, and Sincere rose 64:

➤ Slop: Grok 4.5 (68), Grok 4.6 (38) and Grok 4.7 (6)
➤ Sycophantic: Grok 4.5 (18), Grok 4.6 (3) and Grok 4.7 (1)
➤ Sincere: Grok 4.5 (26), Grok 4.6 (63) and Grok 4.7 (90)

On Tuesday, we brought together partners and friends in San Francisco to launch Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and our new Progress Index

Micah Hill-Smith (@_micah_h) introduced Intelligence Index v5, including two new benchmarks and three upgrades, with greater weighting on agentic coding and science. For the first time, the majority of the Index is based on private test sets or held-out answers.

We also introduced Artificial Analysis Progress Index, which uses item response theory to estimate a general capability score for each model across dozens of evaluations measured over time, including those retired or excluded from the Intelligence Index. It builds on prior work from @EpochAIResearch and @AnthropicAI to place models on a single capability scale. Intelligence Index remains the flagship metric for choosing which current model to use for a use case today; Progress Index is the better tool for plotting trends over time.

George Cameron (@grmcameron) led a discussion with Silas (@silasalberti) from @cognition, Steven (@StevenDillmann) from @Stanford and Terminal-Bench-Science, and our own Declan Jackson about building evaluations as models become more capable.

The evening also covered our work on 3D modeling, personality, cyber defense, custom enterprise evaluations and robotics. Thank you to our speakers, partners and everyone who joined us!

Explore Intelligence Index v5: https://t.co/YI6GbwBUFD
Explore Progress Index: https://t.co/Bdfnpw5mhw

Search is one of the most important tools for agents, and they search very differently to humans. By the end of the year, agents are expected to search the web far more than humans do

The Artificial Analysis Search Index measures the performance, cost and latency of Search APIs across 1700 tasks and three search-specific benchmarks: BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA and AA-Omniscience using the same base model and harness.

Developers can use the Artificial Analysis Search Index to inform their choices when it comes to what search tool their agent should be using. Now you can see who’s #1 while waiting for the bus. Currently Exa (auto) and Perplexity (medium) lead in performances with their best models scoring 80.
